claim: Ribosomes in resting lymphocytes in vitro and in vivo elongate at typical rates for mammalian cells.

evidence: Established scientific knowledge about lymphocyte characteristics

source: While this work was in progress, the Pierre lab described 'SunRiSE', a nearly identical approach, to measure elongation rates in vitro, observing similar puromycylation decay rates following HAR treatment (Argüello et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation of parallel work

claim: The addition of elongation inhibitors to the RTA protocol greatly reduces the leakiness of harringtonine, thereby improving the calculated elongation rate accuracy.
source: While our findings are similar regarding the elongation rates of fibroblasts and lymphocytes, the addition of elongation inhibitors to the protocol (CHX or EME) greatly reduces the leakiness of HAR, thereby improving the calculated elongation rate accuracy.
evidence: Methodological improvement demonstrated in experiments

claim: A significant fraction of ex vivo lymphocytes possess stalled/primed ribosomes that puromycylate nascent chains but do not transit mRNA.
source: RTA revealed exciting facets of lymphocyte translation. We find that a significant fraction of ex vivo lymphocytes possess stalled/primed ribosomes that puromycylate nascent chains but do not transit mRNA.
evidence: Conclusion from RTA experiments on ex vivo cells

claim: Primary neurons possess substantial numbers of stalled ribosomes to facilitate rapid translation upon synaptic signaling.
source: Graber et al., 2013 used the original RPM protocol to show that primary neurons possess substantial numbers of stalled ribosomes, apparently to facilitate rapid translation upon synaptic signaling.
evidence: Cited study on neuronal translation

claim: Prolonged ribosomal stalling has not been described in mammalian cells other than neurons and lymphocytes.
source: Otherwise, to our knowledge, such prolonged ribosomal stalling has not been described in mammalian cells.
evidence: Assessment of literature on ribosome stalling

claim: The improved RTA protocol reveals a 15-fold increase in translation in day 1 activated OT-I T cells vs. resting OT-I T cells.
source: Our improved RTA protocol reveals the dramatic upregulation of protein synthesis by OT-I CD8+ T cells activated in vivo, with a 15-fold increase in translation in day 1 activated OT-I T cells vs. resting OT-I T cells.
evidence: Measured using improved in vivo RPM protocol

claim: Activated T cells divide every 6.8 hours from day 1 to 2 post-VACV-SIINFEKL infection.
source: Activated T cells divide every 6.8 hr from day 1 to 2 post-VACV-SIINFEKL infection.
evidence: Measured using CFSE dilution

claim: The 6.8 hour doubling time is consistent with a prior OT-I study in mice infected with a different SIINFEKL-expressing VACV.
source: This is consistent with a prior OT-I study in mice infected with a different SIINFEKL-expressing VACV (Xiao et al., 2007).
evidence: Comparison with cited study

claim: RTA can be used to measure elongation rates in vivo by intravenous delivery of translation inhibitors.
source: Importantly, by i.v. delivery of translation inhibitors, we show that RTA can be used to measure elongation rates in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated through in vivo experiments

claim: In vivo RTA can be used to study any cell type in animals that can be analyzed ex vivo by flow cytometry.
source: Though we focus on lymphocytes, in vivo RTA can be used to study any cell type in animals that can be analyzed ex vivo by flow cytometry.
evidence: Generalization of methodological applicability

claim: 33% of monosomes in resting in vivo OT-I T cells were puromycylated.
source: After setting the puromycylation:RPL7 ratio in polysomes to 100% (assuming that all ribosomes in the polysome fraction are actively translating), we found that 33% of monosomes in resting in vivo OT-I T cells and 52% of monosomes in day 2 activated OT-I T cells were puromycylated.
evidence: Measured by dot blot analysis of fractionated ribosomes

claim: 52% of monosomes in day 2 activated OT-I T cells were puromycylated.
source: After setting the puromycylation:RPL7 ratio in polysomes to 100% (assuming that all ribosomes in the polysome fraction are actively translating), we found that 33% of monosomes in resting in vivo OT-I T cells and 52% of monosomes in day 2 activated OT-I T cells were puromycylated.
evidence: Measured by dot blot analysis of fractionated ribosomes

claim: Approximately 38% of overall translation occurs in monosomes of resting in vivo OT-I cells, assuming equal elongation rates.
source: Since in vivo RTA indicates that there is essentially no stalling of puromycylated ribosomes (Figure 4C), these data demonstrate robust translation in T cell monosomes. Assuming equal elongation rates, ~38% and ~32% of overall translation would occur in monosomes of resting in vivo and activated in vitro cells, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from puromycylation data and RTA results

claim: Approximately 32% of overall translation occurs in monosomes of activated in vitro OT-I cells, assuming equal elongation rates.
source: Since in vivo RTA indicates that there is essentially no stalling of puromycylated ribosomes (Figure 4C), these data demonstrate robust translation in T cell monosomes. Assuming equal elongation rates, ~38% and ~32% of overall translation would occur in monosomes of resting in vivo and activated in vitro cells, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from puromycylation data and RTA results

claim: A small fraction of translating monosomes probably derive from the polysome population since puromycin reduces the number of polysomes recovered from cycloheximide-treated cells by 5-10%.
source: We note, however, that since PMY reduces the number of polysomes recovered from CHX-treated cells by 5 – 10%, a small fraction of translating monosomes probably derive from the polysome population.
evidence: Observation from polysome profiling experiments

claim: The activation protocol including SIINFEKL antigenic stimulation along with PHA and ionomycin is more effective than PMA/ionomycin alone.
source: We noted that the activation protocol for OT-I T cells we used is far less effective than that published by Tan et al., 2017 which includes SIINFEKL antigenic stimulation along with PHA and ionomycin. Bulk peptide-antigen stimulation directly ex vivo is not possible with human cells, but it is with transgenic murine T cells, and the methodological adaptation enhances activation. Direct comparison of the protocols confirmed the superiority of Tan et al ., as shown by activation markers (CD69, CD25, CD44), cell size (measured by side scatter, which correlates well with automated diameter measurements), and cell division (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Comparative experimental data on activation protocols

claim: OT-I cells activated by the optimized protocol yielded large increases in the observed polysome fractions.
source: OT-I cells activated by this protocol yielded large increases in the observed polysome fractions of activated splenocytes, or lymph-node-derived lymphocytes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Observation from polysome profiling with optimized activation

claim: 500 mM salt was necessary to fully dissociate non-translating ribosomes compared to the often used 300 mM.
source: This was also evident during high salt fractionation conditions, where we found that 500 mM was necessary to fully dissociate non-translating ribosomes compared to the often used 300 mM (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Experimental determination of optimal salt concentration

claim: T cell ribosomes had quantifiable but low levels of monosomes under high salt conditions.
source: T cell ribosomes had quantifiable but low levels of monosomes under these high salt conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D; note that we could not obtain enough activated OT-I cells in vivo for these experiments).
evidence: Observation from high salt polysome profiling

claim: Monosomes make a major contribution to translation in resting T cells.
source: These findings indicate that monosomes make a major contribution to translation in resting T cells but are likely to make a minor contribution in fully activated cells.
evidence: Conclusion from polysome profiling and puromycylation experiments

claim: Monosomes are likely to make a minor contribution to translation in fully activated cells.
source: These findings indicate that monosomes make a major contribution to translation in resting T cells but are likely to make a minor contribution in fully activated cells.
evidence: Conclusion from polysome profiling experiments with optimized activation

claim: Harringtonine may only be useful until 45 seconds after the start of treatment, based on the assumption that polysomes are the only ribosome subset actively translating mRNA.
source: These results might also complicate the conclusion reached by Gerashchenko et al., 2021 that HAR may only be useful until 45 s after the start of treatment, as the assumption was made that polysomes were the only ribosome subset actively translating mRNA.
evidence: Critique of cited study based on monosome translation findings

claim: Cells need to synthesize sufficient proteins to regenerate a complete proteome each division cycle.
source: Cells need to synthesize sufficient proteins to regenerate a complete proteome each division cycle.
evidence: Fundamental principle of cell division

claim: The number of proteins needed depends on the division rate, cell size, protein concentration, and protein loss due to degradation and export.
source: This number will depend on the division rate, cell size, protein concentration, and protein loss due to degradation and export (secretion, release of exosomes, loss of other cellular material).
evidence: Logical factors affecting protein requirements

claim: The optimized protocol for in vitro OT-I T cell activation greatly increased the fraction of ribosomes in polysomes on day 1 post activation.
source: For these experiments, we used the optimized protocol for in vitro OT-I T cell activation (Tan et al., 2017) that greatly increased the fraction of ribosomes in polysomes on day 1 post activation.
evidence: Observation from polysome profiling with optimized protocol

claim: OT-I T cells increase in diameter from the resting state to the day 1 and 2 activated states.
source: Automated microscope measurements revealed that OT-I T cells increase in diameter from the resting state to the day 1 and 2 activated states, with a corresponding calculated volume increase (based on spherical geometry) of ~2.9-fold (Figure 6B).
evidence: Measured using automated cell counter

claim: OT-I T cells have a calculated volume increase of approximately 2.9-fold from resting to day 2 activated state.
source: Automated microscope measurements revealed that OT-I T cells increase in diameter from the resting state to the day 1 and 2 activated states, with a corresponding calculated volume increase (based on spherical geometry) of ~2.9-fold (Figure 6B).
evidence: Calculated from diameter measurements assuming spherical geometry

claim: Protein content per T cell increases approximately fivefold following activation.
source: Protein content per T cell increases ~fivefold following activation (Figure 6C), from 421 million proteins per cell (assuming an average length of 472 aa and a proteome Trp content of 0.69% Wiśniewski and Gaugaz, 2015) to 2.15 billion proteins per cell in day 2 activated cells, resulting in a net 1.7-fold increase in protein concentration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Measured using tryptophan fluorescence method

claim: Resting OT-I T cells contain 421 million proteins per cell.
source: Protein content per T cell increases ~fivefold following activation (Figure 6C), from 421 million proteins per cell (assuming an average length of 472 aa and a proteome Trp content of 0.69% Wiśniewski and Gaugaz, 2015) to 2.15 billion proteins per cell in day 2 activated cells, resulting in a net 1.7-fold increase in protein concentration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Calculated from tryptophan fluorescence measurements with stated assumptions

claim: Day 2 activated OT-I T cells contain 2.15 billion proteins per cell.
source: Protein content per T cell increases ~fivefold following activation (Figure 6C), from 421 million proteins per cell (assuming an average length of 472 aa and a proteome Trp content of 0.69% Wiśniewski and Gaugaz, 2015) to 2.15 billion proteins per cell in day 2 activated cells, resulting in a net 1.7-fold increase in protein concentration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Calculated from tryptophan fluorescence measurements with stated assumptions

claim: There is a net 1.7-fold increase in protein concentration from resting to day 2 activated OT-I T cells.
source: Protein content per T cell increases ~fivefold following activation (Figure 6C), from 421 million proteins per cell (assuming an average length of 472 aa and a proteome Trp content of 0.69% Wiśniewski and Gaugaz, 2015) to 2.15 billion proteins per cell in day 2 activated cells, resulting in a net 1.7-fold increase in protein concentration (Figure 6D).
evidence: Calculated from protein content and volume measurements

claim: The maximal number of translating ribosomes is limited by the less abundant subunit, which in all cases is the 60S subunit.
source: The maximal number of translating ribosomes is limited by the less abundant subunit, which in all cases is the 60S subunit (typically 75–90% of the 40S subunit).
evidence: Observation from ribosome quantification experiments

claim: The 60S subunit is typically 75-90% of the 40S subunit abundance.
source: The maximal number of translating ribosomes is limited by the less abundant subunit, which in all cases is the 60S subunit (typically 75–90% of the 40S subunit).
evidence: Quantitative observation from ribosome measurements

claim: 60S subunits increased to approximately 3.6 million copies per T cell following 2 days in vitro activation from 264,000 copies in resting T cells.
source: 60S subunits increased both in absolute terms and per unit cell volume as T cells became activated, reaching a maximum of ~3.6 million copies per T cell following 2d in vitro activation from 264,000 copies in resting T cells (Figure 6F–G).
evidence: Measured using bioanalyzer-based rRNA quantification

claim: These ribosome numbers are similar to those reported by Wolf et al., 2020, but should be more accurate since Wolf et al. used total cellular RNA content to estimate ribosomes.
source: These numbers are similar to those reported by Wolf et al., 2020, but should be more accurate since Wolf et al. used total cellular RNA content to estimate ribosomes.
evidence: Methodological comparison with cited study

claim: The distribution of ribosomes in lymphocytes is similar in resting and activated OT-I T and HeLa cells, with only a small fraction of total ribosomal subunits detected in nuclear lysates.
source: Immunoblotting of fractionated nuclei shows that the distribution of ribosomes in lymphocytes is similar in resting and activated OT-I T and HeLa cells, with only a small fraction of total ribosomal subunits detected in nuclear lysates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation from cell fractionation and immunoblotting experiments

claim: The ratio of proteins to ribosomes dropped up to threefold as T cells became activated.
source: The ratio of proteins to ribosomes is critical since it dictates the minimal time to replicate the proteome during cell division. This dropped up to threefold as T cells became activated (Figure 6H).
evidence: Calculated from protein and ribosome measurements

claim: Mammalian ribosomes elongate at approximately 6 residues per second.
source: Since mammalian ribosomes elongate at ~6 residues per second (Ingolia et al., 2011; Fan and Penman, 1970), we calculated the minimal time for a ribosome to recreate the proteome based on the protein/maximally assembled ribosome ratios, not accounting for protein degradation or secretion.
evidence: Established rate from cited literature

claim: For HeLa cells, it would take a ribosome 19.9 hours to synthesize 910 average proteins, reasonably close to the reported doubling time of approximately 24 hours.
source: For HeLa cells, it would take a ribosome 19.9 hr to synthesize 910 'average' proteins of 472 amino acids, reasonably close to the reported doubling time of ~24 hr.
evidence: Calculated from measured parameters and compared to known doubling time

claim: For OT-I T cells with an in vitro doubling time of approximately 9.7 hours, the calculated minimal proteome duplication time is 10.1 hours by day 2.
source: For OT-I T cells, with an in vitro doubling time of ~9.7 hr, the calculated minimal proteome duplication time is also within shouting distance – 10.1 hr by day 2.
evidence: Calculated from measured parameters and compared to measured doubling time

claim: Adoptively transferred OT-I T cells divide most rapidly between days 1 and 2 of activation during acute viral infection, with an average doubling time of 6.8 hours.
source: We extended these findings to OT-I T cells in vivo, determining first that adoptively transferred OT-I T cells divide most rapidly between days 1 and 2 of activation during acute viral infection, with an average doubling time of 6.8 hr, slowing to approximately 7.7 hr by day 2 post-infection (via CFSE labeling; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Measured using CFSE dilution in infected mice

claim: The discrepancy is further exacerbated when accounting for protein secretion and degradation of DRiPs (30% of nascent proteins) and retirees with a half-life of approximately 32 hours over the entire proteome.
source: The discrepancy is further exacerbated when accounting for protein secretion and degradation of DRiPs (30% of nascent proteins) (Qian et al., 2005; Princiotta et al., 2003; Schubert et al., 2000; Wheatley et al., 1980) and retirees t½ of ~32 hr over the entire proteome (Doherty et al., 2009; Cambridge et al., 2011) and the presence of stalled and resting ribosomes.
evidence: Consideration of additional factors with cited literature

claim: 30% of nascent proteins are DRiPs (defective ribosomal products).
source: The discrepancy is further exacerbated when accounting for protein secretion and degradation of DRiPs (30% of nascent proteins) (Qian et al., 2005; Princiotta et al., 2003; Schubert et al., 2000; Wheatley et al., 1980) and retirees t½ of ~32 hr over the entire proteome (Doherty et al., 2009; Cambridge et al., 2011) and the presence of stalled and resting ribosomes.
evidence: Established value from cited literature

claim: The proteome has a half-life of approximately 32 hours.
source: The discrepancy is further exacerbated when accounting for protein secretion and degradation of DRiPs (30% of nascent proteins) (Qian et al., 2005; Princiotta et al., 2003; Schubert et al., 2000; Wheatley et al., 1980) and retirees t½ of ~32 hr over the entire proteome (Doherty et al., 2009; Cambridge et al., 2011) and the presence of stalled and resting ribosomes.
evidence: Value from cited literature on protein turnover

claim: Accounting for protein degradation and secretion likely doubles the time required to synthesize the proteome.
source: Together, this likely doubles the time required to synthesize the proteome.
evidence: Estimated impact of protein loss on synthesis requirements

claim: T cell doubling times of 6.8 hours are very likely to be accurate, as they are simple to measure and are routinely reported in mouse T cell studies.
source: T cell doubling times of 6.8 hr are very likely to be accurate, as they are simple to measure and are routinely reported in mouse T cell studies.
evidence: Assessment of measurement reliability

claim: Wolf et al., 2020 mass spectrometric-based measurements of in vitro T cell protein synthetic capacity supports and even exacerbates the paradox.
source: While one or more of these values may yet be inaccurate, we note that Wolf et al., 2020 mass spectrometric-based measurements of in vitro T cell protein synthetic capacity supports and even exacerbates the paradox.
evidence: Comparison with independent measurements from cited study

claim: Lymphocytes may resort to acquiring proteins from resting lymphocytes or other cell types to support their rapid division.
source: We must therefore consider the possibility that that lymphocytes are in such a hurry to divide that they resort to the extraordinary measure of acquiring proteins from resting lymphocytes or other cell types.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis to explain the paradox

claim: Neurons acquire ribosomes from Schwann cells.
source: There are reports that neurons acquire ribosomes from Schwann cells (Court et al., 2008; Court et al., 2011) and that cancer cells acquire mitochondria from immune cells (Saha et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited precedent for intercellular transfer of cellular components

claim: Cancer cells acquire mitochondria from immune cells.
source: There are reports that neurons acquire ribosomes from Schwann cells (Court et al., 2008; Court et al., 2011) and that cancer cells acquire mitochondria from immune cells (Saha et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited precedent for intercellular transfer of cellular components

claim: Lymphocytes acquire cell surface molecules from other cells through trogocytosis.
source: Furthermore, through trogocytosis, lymphocytes acquire cell surface molecules from other cells (Joly and Hudrisier, 2003).
evidence: Cited precedent for lymphocyte acquisition of cellular material

claim: Lymphocytes may acquire a significant fraction of their proteome via something akin to emperipolesis or entosis.
source: We are, however, proposing that lymphocytes acquire a significant fraction of their proteome, perhaps via something akin to emperipolesis or entosis (Yang and Li, 2012), where cells actively enter homotypic cells and can even divide while residing inside (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis with cited mechanisms

claim: In emperipolesis or entosis, cells actively enter homotypic cells and can even divide while residing inside.
source: We are, however, proposing that lymphocytes acquire a significant fraction of their proteome, perhaps via something akin to emperipolesis or entosis (Yang and Li, 2012), where cells actively enter homotypic cells and can even divide while residing inside (Overholtzer et al., 2007).
evidence: Description of cited cellular processes

claim: Much remains to be learned about basic lymphocyte cell biology.
source: In any event, our findings clearly indicate how much remains to be learned about basic lymphocyte cell biology and the importance of simple accounting in squaring our models of cell biology with reality.
evidence: Concluding assessment based on the paradox identified

claim: Simple accounting is important in squaring our models of cell biology with reality.
source: In any event, our findings clearly indicate how much remains to be learned about basic lymphocyte cell biology and the importance of simple accounting in squaring our models of cell biology with reality.
evidence: Methodological lesson from the study

claim: Contrary to recent claims, puromycin does not completely release nascent chains when ribosomes are previously exposed to cycloheximide.
source: The robust PMY signal shows that, contrary to recent claims (Enam et al., 2020; Hobson et al., 2020), PMY does not completely release nascent chains when ribosomes are previously exposed to CHX (Figure 5A).
evidence: Experimental observation contradicting cited claims

claim: Emetine was ineffective in vivo for stabilizing puromycylated polypeptides on ribosomes.
source: Notably, this experiment used our original protocol of PMY treatment alone (Seedhom et al., 2016) since EME, the inhibitor used to stabilize puromycylated polypeptides on ribosomes in vitro (David et al., 2012) was ineffective in vivo.
evidence: Observation from in vivo experiments

claim: Cycloheximide is active in vivo, arresting the accumulation of puromycylated polypeptides for at least 60 minutes after injecting puromycin.
source: We found, however, that CHX is active in vivo, arresting the accumulation of puromycylated polypeptides for at least 60 min after injecting PMY (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental observation from in vivo time course

claim: The number of translating ribosomes varies over a narrow range among resting splenic lymphocytes, NK cells, macrophages, and neutrophils.
source: The number of translating ribosomes varies over a narrow range among resting splenic lymphocytes, NK cells, macrophages, and neutrophils (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Measured using the improved in vivo RPM protocol

claim: Using the improved RPM protocol, there is a approximately 15-fold increase in translating ribosomes in activated OT-I T cells in vivo 1 day after VACV infection.
source: Using this improved RPM protocol, 1 day after infecting mice with VACV we now measured a ~15-fold increase in translating ribosomes in activated OT-I T cells in vivo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; gating strategy in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) as compared to the 10-fold increase we previously reported (Seedhom et al., 2016).
evidence: Measured using improved in vivo RPM protocol

claim: As cell division progressed over 2 days after VACV infection, the signal from translating ribosomes decreased.
source: As cell division progressed over the next 2 days, the signal from translating ribosomes decreased (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Observation from time course of in vivo RPM measurements

claim: A transgenic T cell population has much less spread of RPM staining compared to activated polyclonal T cells.
source: Comparing the results from Figure 4—figure supplement 1C (OT-I cells) with (polyclonal human CD8+ T cells) reveals what we had described previously (Seedhom et al., 2016), that a transgenic T cell population has much less spread of RPM staining when compared to activated polyclonal T cells in C57/BL6J mice after VACV infection, or here when comparing to all human CD8+ T cells.
evidence: Comparative observation between transgenic and polyclonal populations

claim: Addition of cycloheximide to the in vivo RTA is important because of the well-characterized leakiness of harringtonine.
source: We next performed the modified RTA to measure translation rates in OT-I cells in vivo on day 2 and 3 post-infection with VACV-SIINFEKL (Figure 4C). Addition of CHX to the in vivo RTA is important because of the well-characterized 'leakiness' of HAR (Lee et al., 2012); indeed, ribosome transit times in activated OT-I cells were now in line with the in vitro rates, and were ~20% faster than transit times in recipient (non-activated) T cells.
evidence: Methodological justification with cited reference

claim: Ribosome transit times in activated OT-I cells measured with the modified in vivo RTA were in line with in vitro rates.
source: We next performed the modified RTA to measure translation rates in OT-I cells in vivo on day 2 and 3 post-infection with VACV-SIINFEKL (Figure 4C). Addition of CHX to the in vivo RTA is important because of the well-characterized 'leakiness' of HAR (Lee et al., 2012); indeed, ribosome transit times in activated OT-I cells were now in line with the in vitro rates, and were ~20% faster than transit times in recipient (non-activated) T cells.
evidence: Comparison of in vivo and in vitro measurements

claim: Ribosome transit times in activated OT-I cells were approximately 20% faster than transit times in recipient non-activated T cells in vivo.
source: We next performed the modified RTA to measure translation rates in OT-I cells in vivo on day 2 and 3 post-infection with VACV-SIINFEKL (Figure 4C). Addition of CHX to the in vivo RTA is important because of the well-characterized 'leakiness' of HAR (Lee et al., 2012); indeed, ribosome transit times in activated OT-I cells were now in line with the in vitro rates, and were ~20% faster than transit times in recipient (non-activated) T cells.
evidence: Measured using modified in vivo RTA

claim: The elongation rate in vivo is surprisingly slower than the in vitro rate when measured without cycloheximide.
source: The elongation rate in vivo is surprisingly slower than the in vitro rate.
evidence: Observation from initial in vivo RTA experiments

claim: If ribosomes in in vivo activated T cells are translating at 7.8 residues per second, the time required to synthesize the proteome is 2.3 times greater than the observed replication time (15.5 vs. 6.8 hours).
source: Even if ribosomes in in vivo activated T cells are translating at 7.8 residues per second, the time required to synthesize the proteome is 2.3× greater than the observed replication time (15.5 vs. 6.8 hr).
evidence: Calculated using the higher elongation rate observed in vivo
